content: Infantile colic significantly impacts both infants and their parents, often leaving parents feeling exhausted and distressed as they try to soothe their crying child. Traditional approaches to managing colic have focused on physical treatments aimed at reducing symptoms, but the evidence supporting their effectiveness remains inconclusive. An alternative strategy involves providing parents with training, support, and psychological interventions, collectively referred to as parent training programmes. These programmes may include techniques for soothing crying infants, feeding advice, or educational materials aimed at normalizing the experience of colic. The delivery methods for these programmes vary and can include in-person courses, online resources, printed materials, home visits, or remote counseling. The goal of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of such interventions in reducing colic symptoms and parental anxiety, as well as to identify the educational content and characteristics of these programmes. The objectives of the review were twofold: first, to assess the effectiveness and safety of parent training programmes for managing colic in infants under four months of age, and second, to identify the specific educational content and features of these programmes. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in June 2019 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and 13 others, as well as two trial registries. Additional efforts included hand-searching conference abstracts, reviewing references of included studies, and contacting experts in the field to identify further trials. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that evaluated the effectiveness of any form of parent training programme, either alone or in combination with other interventions, compared to alternative interventions or control groups, in managing infantile colic. Two authors independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Data analysis was performed using Review Manager 5, and the certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE methodology. The search yielded 6064 records, of which 20 were selected for full-text review. Ultimately, seven studies involving a total of 1187 participants met the inclusion criteria. All studies focused on infants under four months of age with colic. Four studies were conducted in the United States, one in Canada, one in the Netherlands, and one in Iran. Funding sources were reported in four studies and included national research institutes, foundations, and nutritional companies. Five studies compared parent training programmes to control groups that received either reassurance or routine care. One of these studies also included a third arm that evaluated the use of a specialized baby seat. Another study compared parent training to a milk-exclusion diet, while a third compared parent training alone to parent training combined with swaddling. The duration of the interventions ranged from six days to three months. Most studies had small sample sizes and were at high risk of bias, including selection bias, performance bias, and potential placebo effects. Due to insufficient data in the study reports and a lack of additional information from authors, the planned qualitative analysis of the educational content and attributes of the programmes could not be completed. Instead, a descriptive content analysis was performed using the limited available information. The parent training interventions addressed one or more of the following areas: soothing techniques for crying infants (six studies), general care advice including sleep (four studies), feeding advice (two studies), stress reduction and empathetic support for parents (two studies), and positive play interaction advice (one study). One study specifically taught kangaroo care, a method of skin-to-skin contact. Control groups received reassurance (two studies), advice to rock the infant in a crib (one study), or no intervention (two studies). A meta-analysis of three studies involving 157 infants assessed the primary outcome of crying time at the end of the study period. Parent training was found to be more effective than control, with a mean difference (MD) of −113.58 minutes per day (95% confidence interval [CI]: −144.19 to −82.96 minutes per day). However, the certainty of this evidence was low due to imprecision and concerns about bias. One study with 38 participants compared parent training to the use of a specialized baby seat and found no significant difference in crying time, though specific figures were not reported. Another study with 20 participants compared parent training to a milk-exclusion or soy milk formula diet, reporting crying times of 2.03 hours and 1.08 hours, respectively, at the end of the study. A study involving 398 participants compared parent training alone to parent training combined with swaddling but did not report separate data for each group. No adverse effects were reported in any of the studies, although adverse events were not explicitly addressed. In conclusion, the evidence on the effectiveness and safety of parent training programmes for managing infantile colic is limited. While one meta-analysis suggested that parent training may reduce crying times compared to control, the certainty of this evidence is low. Evidence from other comparisons is sparse, and the educational content and attributes of the programmes could not be comprehensively identified due to insufficient data. Further high-quality RCTs are needed to clearly define interventions, address relevant outcomes, and minimize bias in order to determine the definitive role of parent training programmes in managing infantile colic.
